key_terms.meaning: K = y*/x, the solute concentration in the extract divided by its equilibrium concentration in the raffinate, both on the same basis (mass ratio or mass fraction).
The boundary curve on a ternary diagram; mixtures inside it split into two liquid layers, mixtures outside stay single-phase.
A straight line joining the two equilibrium liquid compositions that coexist on the binodal curve.
The point on the binodal curve where the two phases become identical, so extract and raffinate compositions merge and tie lines vanish.
β = (solute/solvent ratio in extract) ÷ (solute/carrier ratio in raffinate); β well above 1 means the solvent picks the solute and leaves the carrier.
E = K·S/R, where K is the distribution coefficient, S the solvent flow and R the raffinate (carrier) flow; E is the solvent strength relative to the liquid it must treat.
Fresh solvent contacts the raffinate in each stage; the extracts leave separately and are pooled afterwards.
x<sub>n</sub> = x<sub>0</sub>/(1 + E)<sup>n</sup> for constant E, where x<sub>0</sub> is the feed solute ratio and x<sub>n</sub> the raffinate ratio after n stages.
The straight line from a solute balance around stages 1 to n, linking the raffinate leaving stage n to the solvent entering stage n+1.
The pole where the operating lines of all stages meet; it fixes the stage stepping on the triangular diagram.
A graphical stage count on a right-angle ternary plot: locate feed, solvent and Δ, then step between the equilibrium (tie line) and operating lines.
The smallest solvent flow at which the operating line just touches the equilibrium curve; it needs infinite stages, so design uses 1.2 to 2 times this value.
A stirred vessel that disperses one liquid in the other, followed by a quiet settler that lets the two layers separate; one unit is roughly one equilibrium stage.
An agitated extraction column with discs on a central shaft that shear the rising or falling drops, giving high interfacial area in a short height.
For leaching, N = mass inert solid ÷ mass solution retained, X = mass solute ÷ mass solvent, and all balances are written on the inert solid B, which never leaves.
Ideal (equilibrium) stages divided by actual stages needed for the same separation; real stages are 60 to 90 per cent efficient at best.
A packed or sieve-plate column in which a reciprocating pulse of liquid adds agitation and interfacial area without moving parts inside the column.
Extraction with a fluid held above its critical temperature and pressure, whose density and solvent power change steeply with pressure alone.
Solvent is sprayed on a stationary bed of crushed solids and drains through the bed, dissolving solute as it flows.
A battery of tanks where the same liquid is pumped tank to tank against the solids, so each tank meets a stronger or weaker solution and fresh solvent is needed only once.

takeaways: Extraction works only when the solvent dissolves the solute far better than the carrier and the two phases settle apart quickly.
The triangular ternary diagram converts a two-liquid mixture into a picture from which equilibrium splits and stage counts can be read off.
One equilibrium stage gives one split; repeating contact with fresh solvent in cross-current mode drops solute geometrically, according to x<sub>n</sub> = x<sub>0</sub>/(1 + E)<sup>n</sup>.
Counter-current contact lets each stage meet richer solvent, so it achieves the same recovery with fewer stages and less solvent than cross-current.
Every extractor must do two jobs, disperse the phases for area and coalesce them for separation, and each equipment type balances those two jobs differently.
A leaching balance is written on the inert solid because the spent solid always leaves carrying some solution with it.
Pulsation, centrifugal fields and supercritical solvents are used when a plain column is too tall, too slow or too impure for a heat-sensitive solute.
Percolation, moving beds and the Shanks battery all cost out on the same multistage leaching balance, with actual stages found by dividing ideal stages by stage efficiency.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are graphical stage counts plus a balance check: draw the ternary or right-angled diagram correctly, then report ideal stages, solvent rate and a stage-efficiency correction for the real battery.

bank.q: Explain what a triangular ternary diagram shows for a partly miscible liquid pair, and how the binodal curve, tie lines, plait point and distribution coefficient are read from it.
outline: Axes and the three components labelled
Single-phase region outside the binodal curve, two-phase inside
Tie lines give the two equilibrium compositions; plait point where tie lines shrink to zero
K = y*/x from the ends of a tie line
Effect of temperature on solubility

bank.q: List the characteristics a good liquid extraction solvent must have and explain why each one matters.
outline: High selectivity for the solute over the carrier
High K or high capacity so solvent flow stays small
Low solubility of the carrier in the solvent
Adequate density difference for settling
Low viscosity, low surface tension, low cost, low toxicity, easy recovery by distillation

bank.q: Explain why cross-current extraction needs more solvent and more stages than counter-current extraction for the same solute recovery.
outline: Cross-current: each stage meets fresh solvent, so raffinate contact liquid is weak
Counter-current: solvent leaving stage 1 is richest, and every later stage meets a partly loaded solvent
Operating line and driving force comparison
Geometric drop versus exponential drop
Consequence for solvent recovery cost

bank.q: Describe a mixer-settler unit with a sketch, and state how mixing and settling duties are balanced in its design.
outline: Mixer with impeller, baffles, dispersion of one phase in the other
Settler with residence time for coalescence and a dispersion band
One unit approximates one equilibrium stage
Basis of scale-up: mixer power and settler area
Advantages: simple, flexible; drawback: large floor area and solvent inventory

bank.q: Explain the mechanism of leaching from a porous solid, and why the balance must be written on an inert-solid basis.
outline: Solvent penetrates the pores, solute dissolves, solution diffuses back out
Spent solid leaves wet, always carrying solution away
Definitions of N, X and Y
Inert solid B is conserved, so it is the reference for balances
Difference between leaching and simple washing

bank.q: A single equilibrium stage contacts 1000 kg/h of a feed containing 25 mass per cent solute in a carrier with 500 kg/h of pure solvent. Take K = 2.0 on a mass-ratio basis and find the solute recovered and the extract and raffinate compositions.
outline: Convert feed to solute-free carrier and solute mass ratios
Write the solute balance and the equilibrium relation
Solve for the common equilibrium ratio
Report extract and raffinate flows and compositions
Recovery as a percentage of solute in feed

bank.q: Three cross-current stages each use 400 kg of fresh solvent on 1200 kg/h of feed containing 20 mass per cent solute, with E = 1.5 in each stage. Find the final raffinate composition, the solute recovered and the total solvent used.
outline: Compute E from the given data
Apply x<sub>n</sub> = x<sub>0</sub>/(1 + E)<sup>n</sup> for n = 3
Convert back to mass fractions aquare
Recovery from the difference between feed and final raffinate solute
Comment on the solvent cost of adding stages

bank.q: A counter-current extractor treats a feed of 40 mass per cent solute in carrier with pure solvent. Using the right-angled triangular method, determine the number of theoretical stages for a raffinate containing 3 per cent solute.
outline: Plot the ternary data as a right-angled triangle with the binodal curve and tie lines
Locate the feed point and the solvent point
Fix the difference point Δ from the overall balance
Draw operating lines from Δ and step off stages between tie lines and operating lines
Count and round up the stages, stating the raffinate composition reached

bank.q: 1000 kg of crushed solid containing 20 mass per cent oil and 80 per cent insoluble matter is leached in one stage with 600 kg of solvent. The underflow retains 1.5 kg of solution per kg of insoluble solid. Find the oil recovered and the composition of the retained solution.
outline: Take the inert solid B = 800 kg as reference
Write N = B/solution retained and get solution retained = 800/1.5
Set up solute balance with X in underflow and Y in overflow
Assume equilibrium, X = Y
Report oil recovered and per cent recovery

bank.q: A Shanks battery of tanks treats solids containing solute with fresh solvent entering at the last tank and the concentrated solution leaving at the first. Set up the counter-current leaching balance and determine the number of tanks needed for 95 per cent recovery.
outline: Inert-solid basis and constant solution retention per kg solid
Overall and stage-wise solute balances
Kremser-type relation for constant retention ratio
Solve for n and round up
Compare with cross-current washing for the same duty

bank.q: Compare cross-current and counter-current extraction for a fixed feed and recovery, and justify which one you would recommend when solvent recovery by distillation is expensive.
outline: Stages versus solvent trade-off for each mode
Solvent-to-feed ratio at minimum and at operating value
Effect on extract concentration and distillation load
Capital cost of extra stages versus running cost of solvent recovery
Recommendation with numbers from the calculation

bank.q: For a system whose two liquid phases differ only slightly in density and tend to emulsify, choose between a mixer-settler, a packed column, a pulsed column and a centrifugal extractor, giving reasons.
outline: Small density difference means slow gravity settling
Packed column poor for emulsifying systems and low throughput
Pulsed column adds agitation but still relies on gravity
Centrifugal extractor replaces gravity with a strong field and handles emulsions
Trade-off: capital cost, maintenance, solvent inventory, hygiene and scale

bank.q: Explain how pressure and temperature set the solvent power of a supercritical fluid, and evaluate why supercritical carbon dioxide suits decaffeination and aroma recovery.
outline: Definition of critical point and supercritical region
Density rises steeply with pressure near the critical point
Solubility tracks density, so pressure tunes selectivity
Low critical temperature protects heat-sensitive solutes
Easy solute recovery by pressure let-down, no solvent residue

bank.q: Actual leaching batteries need more stages than the ideal count. Analyse the sources of stage inefficiency in leaching and explain how stage efficiency is applied in design.
outline: Incomplete equilibrium between retained solution and bulk solution
Slow diffusion out of pores and dead-end pores
Channelling in percolation beds and bypassing of solids
Definition: efficiency = ideal stages/actual stages
Design margin, residence time and comparison with extraction stage efficiency

glossary.def: The substance being moved from one phase to the other, for example oil leaving seed or caffeine leaving coffee beans.
The liquid in which the solute is originally dissolved and which the solvent should not dissolve.
The solvent-rich phase leaving a stage, carrying the solute that has been removed.
The carrier-rich phase left behind after the solute has partly moved into the solvent.
The equilibrium ratio of solute concentration in the extract to that in the raffinate at the same temperature.
A triangular composition plot for three components, read either as mass or mole fractions summing to one.
The pair of liquid compositions at the two ends of a tie line, in equilibrium with each other.
A measure of how strongly the solvent prefers the solute over the carrier; a value of one means no separation is possible.
E = K·S/R, the ratio of solute carried by the solvent to solute left in the raffinate per stage.
Feed and solvent flow in the same direction and separate after one contact; limited to one equilibrium split per contact.
Feed and solvent flow in opposite directions through a train of stages, so the richest solvent meets the richest feed.
Part of the extract is returned to the top of the column to raise product purity, at the cost of more stages and solvent.
The mixed layer between the two clear phases in a settler where drops are still coalescing.
The condition in an extraction column where one phase can no longer flow past the other and the column stops working.
A vertical column filled with packing that breaks the dispersed phase into drops and gives contacting area.
A machine that spins the two liquids so the heavier phase separates in seconds instead of hours.
A fluid above both its critical temperature and pressure, with liquid-like density and gas-like viscosity and diffusivity.
Removal of a soluble substance from a solid by contact with a liquid solvent, also called solid-liquid extraction.
The insoluble part of the solid that stays unchanged and is used as the balance reference in leaching calculations.
The spent solid stream leaving a leaching stage, wet with retained solution.
The clear solution stream leaving a leaching stage, carrying the dissolved solute.
Passing solvent down through a stationary bed of solids so it dissolves solute on the way.
Solids travel slowly through a vessel while solvent flows against them, giving continuous counter-current contact.
A set of tanks in which solid is shifted tank to tank while liquid is pumped the other way, approximating counter-current leaching.
A graphical construction using an enthalpy-composition plot that gives stages and energy duties together.
